name: Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current
title: Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current
answer: Keeping comparable company sets current means maintaining a peer group used for valuation, relative performance, and sector benchmarking as the underlying companies change. In finance, a comparable set is only useful if it reflects the current business mix, size, and listing status of each member. The work covers adding new listings, removing acquired or delisted companies, and reclassifying firms when their revenue mix shifts. It also covers documenting why each change was made so that historical analysis remains reproducible.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Keeping comparable company sets current means maintaining a peer group used for valuation, relative performance, and sector benchmarking as the underlying companies change. In finance, a comparable set is only useful if it reflects the current business mix, size, and listing status of each member. The work covers adding new listings, removing acquired or delisted companies, and reclassifying firms when their revenue mix shifts. It also covers documenting why each change was made so that historical analysis remains reproducible.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a combination of market data feeds, regulatory filings, and a maintained company master. This site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices and 355 merger and acquisition filings, which are the kinds of inputs an agent workflow would monitor. Agents need scheduled access to those sources, a place to store the current peer set, and a version history. A typical setup uses a database for the set, a queue for incoming events, and a dashboard for human review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with a rule set that defines what makes a company comparable, such as sector, size, revenue model, and geography. Agents then watch for events that break those rules, including acquisitions, index changes, and new filings. When an event arrives, the agent proposes an update, such as removing a target or adding an acquirer, and attaches the source document. A human analyst reviews the proposal, and the change is committed with a timestamp and a reason code. Periodic full reviews catch slow drift that event triggers miss.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance means every change to the peer set should point back to a filing, a price record, or a documented analyst decision. Rights matter because market data and filings carry license terms that limit redistribution and automated use. Risk includes stale sets that mislead valuation, survivorship bias when failed companies are dropped without a trace, and look-ahead bias when a set is updated with information not available at the time. An audit trail that records who changed what and when is the main control. The site's 148 active AI lawsuits show why legal status can itself be a reason to reclassify a peer.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Agent workflows for peer sets are moving from nightly batch updates to event-driven updates that react within minutes of a filing. Language models are being used to read filings and extract the facts that trigger a reclassification, though human review remains the norm for material changes. Expect tighter integration between the peer set, the valuation model, and the compliance record so that a change in one propagates with a full audit trail. The growth of AI-related litigation and regulation will likely make legal status a standard field in peer definitions. The goal is a set that is current, sourced, and explainable.
